courseTitle: 100 Days of Code: JavaScript Data Structures and Algorithms

lectures.title: What is Queue? Why we need it?

cues.en: All right.
In this section we are going to start to learn a new data structure, which is called Q.
Now by definition, a Q is a data structure that store items in a first in and first out manner.
So what does it mean?
Let's see it in real life.
Example.
As you would have guessed, the Q is same as the real life Q that we see in our daily life.
So here we see the bunch of people from the queue to buy a new iPhone from the Apple Store.
So the Q data structure is also very similar to the Q that we see over here.
So let's closely observe the common features of this Q over here.
The first feature is that if someone wants to buy a new iPhone, he or she has to stay at the end of
the queue over here.
So it's obvious that he or she cannot join the queue from the beginning of the queue or from the middle
of the queue, so they have to join from the end of the queue.
This means that a new addition to this queue happens at the end of the queue.
Now, the next feature is that a person who is at the beginning of the queue will buy a new iPhone first,
so this means that she will be served first.
Then the second person will get the new iPhone, then the third, then fourth, and it continues like
this.
So it always starts from the first person that comes to the queue.
So if we summarize these two features over here, we can see that we are following Fifo method which
means that first in first out this means whoever comes first goes out first.
So in this queue this lady over here came first.
And she will get the iPhone first as soon as the stores open, then the second one, then the third
one.
Now if you compare this behaviour of real life queue with the queue data structure, we can see that
in the queue data structure.
Also we are following the Fifo method, which means that whichever elements comes to the queue first
is going to go out first.
So let's see in our queue, if we want to insert 40, it's going to be inserted at the end of the queue.
So from here you can see that this is the front of queue and this is the end of Q.
Now, if we want to insert the next element one more time, it's going to be inserted at the end of
the Q, always.
Now it's obvious that we cannot insert any element at the middle of this q over here because q follows
the Fifo method.
So this means that the new element will be inserted at the end of the q.
Now if we want to take an element from the q, the first element which is ten over here is going to
come out from the q.
Then the second element will come, then the third element, and it continues like this until we remove
all elements from the q.
So hopefully with these examples you understood the concept of the q.
Now let's see why we need a Q data structure.
So in this case when you need to create an application which utilize first coming data first, then
we need to use the Q data structure.
Q data structure, as the name suggests, is used whenever we need to manage a group of objects in an
order which the first one coming in also gets out first, while others wait for their turns.
Now, a real life example of this application can be point of sale system of the restaurant, it's obvious
that the orders must be processed in the order they received.
As an order is received, it writes to the back of the queue and reads order from the front of the queue
by the cook's device.
So this allows cooks to cook the meals in order they receive.
Another example can be serving requests on a single shared resource like a printer, CPU and task scheduler.
So whenever we are sending a document to the shared printer, it's going to put them in the queue and
the first one that comes will be printed first in real life scenario.
Also, call center phone system uses the queue data structure to hold people calling them in order until
a service representative is free.
So whenever you call the call center, the people that called before are served first, then you will
be served when the next operator is available.
Now, these are the real life applications of the queue data structures where the logic is same as with
the queue data structure.
So with these examples, hopefully everything is clear about what the queue data structure and why we
need it.
